profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting within the AI-Mind European project, where the team is evaluating a draft health technology assessment framework tailored to AI-based tools for early dementia diagnosis. The context is that the draft will be sent next to a small Delphi-style expert panel, so the participants are reviewing whether the framework's domains, examples, and guidance notes are sufficiently complete and appropriately framed for AI-relevant HTA topics such as validation, workflow fit, costs, and equity. The agenda is to review the current draft structure, check whether the clinical pathway example and economic sections are adequate, and decide whether the document is ready to circulate with minor edits. The expected outcome is a provisional approval of the draft for external review, along with a short list of revisions and who will supply supporting material.

members.name: Dr. Elena Varga
members.expertise: Health technology assessment methods, evidence frameworks, reimbursement-facing evaluation design
members.background: A public health researcher who previously worked with European HTA collaborations and now leads the assessment-framework work package for AI-Mind.
members.private_state: She wants the framework to be credible to national HTA bodies and usable beyond this project, while still moving quickly enough to keep the Delphi timeline. She is trying to avoid turning the draft into an over-detailed instrument before external feedback, but she also wants the document to quietly steer the consortium toward evidence that would matter in real adoption decisions.
hidden_assumptions: The framework's real audience is future HTA agencies and hospital adoption committees, not just the current consortium.
External validation evidence should come from settings and data-generation processes meaningfully outside the project's development environment.
Implementation costs naturally include site-level organizational changes such as staff training, referral-pathway adjustments, and clinician time.
A draft can be considered ready for expert review once the domains and examples are stable, even if operational wording is still somewhat provisional.

members.name: Prof. Jonas Lindholm
members.expertise: Neurology, digital biomarkers, multicenter clinical AI deployment
members.background: A neurologist and clinical researcher overseeing how the AI-Mind tools connect to memory-clinic practice and how project evidence is translated into implementation plans.
members.private_state: He wants the framework to reflect what the consortium can realistically evidence within the project and to avoid adding expectations that local clinics cannot yet satisfy. He also wants the draft to look concrete enough that external experts view the project as implementation-oriented rather than purely methodological.
hidden_assumptions: The framework's immediate purpose is to structure and showcase evidence the AI-Mind consortium itself will generate over the next project phases.
External validation can reasonably include held-out consortium sites that were not used for model training or tuning.
Implementation costs mainly refer to the technical deployment package, while broader service redesign belongs to later implementation work rather than the core HTA template.
A document is ready to circulate only if item wording is already specific enough that clinicians from different countries will interpret each prompt similarly.
When project colleagues mention the pilot workflow, they usually mean the currently used multicenter study workflow rather than a future routine-care pathway.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer positively to including 'external validation evidence' in the framework.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means evidence from a genuinely independent care context outside the model-development environment, ideally with different operational conditions than the consortium's own development pathway.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means performance results from consortium sites that were held out from training, because they are external to the model-building dataset even if they are still inside AI-Mind.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'external validation' is standard and sounds precise, so neither expects that the other is using a narrower or broader HTA-oriented meaning; both can cite real sites and data while believing they are talking about the same evidence category.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included under implementation costs
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the framework should capture 'implementation costs' for the AI tool.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes software licensing, infrastructure, clinician training time, changes to referral logistics, confirmatory testing triggered downstream, and local workflow adaptation burdens on adopting services.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the technical deployment package such as cloud hosting, device maintenance, integration effort, and consumables, but not broader clinic reorganization or pathway redesign costs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Implementation costs are routinely discussed as a single basket term, and both participants have overlapping examples at the top level; the disagreement is only about where the boundary of the basket sits, so surface agreement feels sufficient.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'pilot workflow' is being used as the example pathway
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss using 'the pilot workflow' as a concrete example in the framework notes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the planned future routine-care pilot pathway in memory-clinic deployment, where the tool sits within referral and follow-up decisions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current AI-Mind multicenter study workflow used for recruitment, EEG capture, and retrospective/prospective validation activities at partner sites.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the project, both workflows have been called 'the pilot' in different meetings, so the shorthand sounds shared and natural; because both are dementia-screening pathways involving the same partners, the mismatch is easy to miss.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready for the expert round' means
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the draft should be 'ready for the expert round' after this review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks ready means the topic domains, section order, and a few examples are stable enough for experts to react to, with wording refinement expected afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks ready means the prompts are already specific and operational enough that external panelists from different countries will interpret them consistently without much ambiguity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'ready' often functions as a routine milestone label rather than a debated criterion; both participants want to move forward, so the phrase carries a false sense of shared completion standards.

turns.inner_thought: If the domains, ordering, and examples are stable, that is enough for the Delphi panel. I do not want us trapped polishing operational wording for weeks before getting outside reactions. The real test is whether HTA-facing reviewers can see the structure and respond to it as a credible assessment framework, not whether every line is yet instrument-grade.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The main purpose today is fairly practical: to decide whether this AI-specific HTA draft is ready for the expert round, with only minor edits before we circulate it. I think the structure is largely there, so I'd like us to focus on the few sections that may still need tightening.

turns.inner_thought: From my side the framework is close, but I do not want clinicians on the panel seeing loose prompts and concluding we are still too abstract. The places most likely to matter are external validation and the pilot workflow, because those are where reviewers will look for evidence that the consortium can actually support and explain consistently across sites.
turns.utterance: From the clinical side, I agree the overall structure looks strong. For me, the main question is whether the sections on external validation and the pilot workflow are already clear enough that reviewers will immediately understand what we are asking them to react to.

turns.inner_thought: I need one sentence that nudges the framework toward validation evidence that stands outside the project's own development environment, without turning this into a lecture. And the pilot workflow example should show how the tool sits in a future care pathway, so experts think in terms of referral, review, and follow-up rather than only study procedures.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that is manageable. Under external validation evidence, we could add one short clarifying sentence, and then use the pilot workflow example to make the care-fit aspect more visible. That should help reviewers anchor the framework in something concrete without overloading the draft.

turns.inner_thought: We already have enough to make this concrete through the held-out Helsinki and Turku results, and the multicenter study pathway is familiar to all the sites. That is exactly the sort of material that shows this is not just theoretical. I hope we do not drift into asking for examples that sit beyond what the project can currently demonstrate.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me. On the evidence side, the Helsinki and Turku material already gives us a concrete basis for the external validation part, and the current pilot workflow is detailed enough that we can use it in the notes without inventing anything new.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to keep the cost section broad enough that it signals the full adoption burden, including training, service adjustments, and downstream effects, but without trying to quantify everything yet. At this stage the framework only needs the right buckets. If we start itemizing too deeply before expert input, we will stall.
turns.utterance: Good. Then on the economics side, my view is that implementation costs only need to be framed at a sensible high level in this version. We should make sure the category is clearly present, but I do not think we need a highly granular treatment before the expert round.

turns.inner_thought: That suits me. We can readily point to the deployment package items we actually know: licensing, hosting, hardware upkeep, integration work. If we stay with that level now, the framework will look practical and evidence-linked, without opening broad questions about clinic reorganization that local sites cannot yet answer.
turns.utterance: Yes, agreed. We can list the obvious components now—license fees, cloud hosting, EEG-cap replacement, integration effort—and then add fuller figures later where we have them. That should make the implementation costs section concrete enough for this stage.

turns.inner_thought: I want to lock the domains and examples today and move on. The expert panel can help sharpen the wording. If I let 'ready' become synonymous with fully standardized phrasing, we will miss the Delphi window and lose the chance to let external reviewers shape the framework while it is still flexible.
turns.utterance: Exactly. If we can fix the domains and examples today, I would consider the document ready for the expert round, even if a few explanatory notes still get polished afterward. I do not think that should hold up circulation.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that as long as the prompts themselves are specific enough that people in different countries read them the same way. External experts will be unforgiving if terms like validation, fairness, or workflow fit are left too open. I need this to look implementation-oriented and disciplined, not just conceptually promising.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I would just say that external experts will particularly appreciate wording that already points them toward validation, fairness, and workflow interpretation in a consistent way. If we keep those prompts crisp, the draft should land well.

turns.inner_thought: So the revisions are modest: a sentence steering external validation toward the sort of evidence HTA audiences expect, a worked pathway example using the future pilot workflow in care terms, and a slightly broader note on implementation costs so reviewers can see that adoption consequences extend beyond the software alone. That is enough for circulation.
turns.utterance: Let me summarize the revisions, then. We add a short clarification on external validation, include a worked example based on the pilot workflow, and briefly expand the note on implementation costs. If we do those three things, I think the draft is in very good shape.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the multicenter study workflow documents and the deployment budget inputs from the sites, and that should be enough to finalize this week. From my perspective, once those concrete materials are inserted, the framework will look ready and grounded in what AI-Mind can actually deliver soon.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I can send over the site material from the pilot and the deployment-budget inputs this afternoon, and then we should be able to get the revised draft out this week. That feels like a sensible way to make it ready for the expert round without slowing ourselves down.
